list.listitem: No gold standard test exists for diagnosis of Kawasaki disease (KD). Diagnosis must be made based on clinical features and, if there is atypical presentation, include supportive laboratory work and echocardiogram. C
Treatment for the disease is aimed at decreasing systemic inflammation, prevention of the development of coronary aneurysms, and prevention of thromboses in the coronary arteries. A
Main treatment of KD consists of IVIG and aspirin therapy. A
Recommendations for long-term management are based on a risk stratification system. C

background.definition: KD, also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, is an acute febrile illness in children, caused by a systemic vasculitis that has a predilection for midsize arteries, particularly the coronary arteries.

list.listitem: 9 to 20 per 100,000 children under the age of 5 in the United States. Incidence is 2.5 times higher in Asians and Pacific Islanders under 5 years of age, and 1.5 times higher in those of African American descent
The ratio of males to females is around 1.5 to 1.0
KD has replaced acute rheumatic fever as the most common cause of acquired heart disease in children in the United States.
Recurrence is possible. In Japan, the recurrence rate is estimated at 3%.
No causative agent has been found to date.
Seasonality and tendency to cluster within communities suggest an infectious etiology.
Familial occurrence, with a 10 fold increase in incidence in siblings, suggests a genetic component to the disease as well.

A significant number of children less than five years of age with a diagnosis of multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C), a post infectious syndrome of SARS-CoV-2, also meet criteria of KD.
Endothelial and smooth muscle cells in medium-sized arteries become edematous with infiltration of inflammatory cells.
During this process, the vessel wall loses structural integrity and weakens, resulting in the formation of an aneurysm.
Aneurysm formation typically occurs in the coronary arteries; however, aneurysms can form in the celiac, mesenteric, femoral, renal, and other arteries as well.
As vessels heal, lesions become fibrotic and stenotic, reducing blood flow and predisposing these areas to chronic thrombus formation.
Assess for clinical features of KD (). C
If clinical situation is suspicious for KD, but patient does not meet the classical criteria for KD, laboratory work for markers of systemic inflammation (ESR and CRP) should be sent.C
Supplemental laboratory work including a CBC, urinalysis, albumin, and alanine aminotransferase are recommended to aid in the diagnosis. C
Patients whose illness does not meet the above KD case definition but have fever and coronary artery abnormalities are classified as having atypical or incomplete KD. C
An additional diagnosis of MIS-C should be considered in any patient with KD and a history of recent SARS-CoV-2 infection. C

list.listitem: Refer to for diagnostic criteria.

In addition to the findings mentioned in , patients typically present with extreme irritability. They may also have symptoms of cardiovascular involvement, arthritis, arthralgias, abdominal pain, diarrhea, aseptic meningitis, hepatic dysfunction, sterile pyuria, urethritis, and uveitis.

Adopted in 2004 and revised in 2017, the American Heart Association in conjunction with the American Academy of Pediatrics put forth a set of guidelines to aid physicians in making the diagnosis of incomplete KD. and Table 2 have been adapted from these guidelines and review the decision process for diagnosing and treating KD.
In addition to those given in , further recommendations for specific groups of patients are given below.
In infants <6 months of age who have had fever for 7 days or longer without any other source, an echocardiogram should be performed to evaluate for KD.
Patients with persistent fevers but who do not meet at least 2 or 3 of the clinical criteria for KD should be reassessed periodically for KD.

Patients who have fever and clinical characteristics of KD, but do not have laboratory evidence of systemic inflammation () require daily follow-up. If fevers persist for 2 or more days, patients should be reevaluated for possibility of KD. If fever resolves and peeling of the skin occurs, patients should be evaluated by echocardiogram for the presence of changes within the coronary arteries.

A positive echocardiogram is indicated by any of the following features: (1) left anterior descending (LAD) or right coronary artery (RCA) diameter ≥2.5 SD over mean for body surface area, (2) coronary arteries that meet the Japanese Ministry of Health criteria for aneurysms, or (3) 3 or more other suggestive features, such as perivascular brightness, lack of tapering, decreased left ventricular function, mitral regurgitation, or z score in LAD or RCA of 2 to 2.5.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation and management of the child with suspected KD.
Initial treatment is a single dose of intravenous gammaglobulin (IVIG) at a dose of 2 g/kg and high-dose aspirin in the acute phase of the illness. A
Give low-dose aspirin for at least 6-8 weeks after discontinuation of high-dose aspirin. C
Anticoagulant therapy with warfarin or low-molecular-weight heparin should be added for patients with coronary artery aneurysms. C
Refractory KD should be treated with a second dose of IVIG. IVIG + steroids are an alternative for refractory Kawasaki disease. C

Initial treatment consists of IVIG at a single dose of 2 g/kg given with ASA within 10 days of the onset of symptoms. Research shows that IVIG reduces the prevalence of coronary artery aneurysms from 25% to around 4%. Those with delayed diagnosis after 10 days of symptom onset should still be considered for treatment if they have evidence of continued systemic inflammation, evidenced by persistent fever, coronary artery aneurysms, and elevated ESR or CRP.
In addition to IVIG, patients should be started on moderate (30-50mg/kg/day) to high-dose aspirin therapy (80-100 mg/kg/day) for its anti-inflammatory and antiplatelet effects until afebrile.

Length of high-dose aspirin therapy varies; some institutions recommend treatment for a minimum of 14 days, but others discontinue high-dose aspirin when the child has been afebrile for 48 to 72 hours. It should be noted that while this is commonly accepted therapy based on clinical experience, evidence from clinical trials is limited. In one RCT involving 134 children less than 6 years of age with KD, IVIG alone was noninferior to IVIG plus high-dose aspirin for coronary artery lesions at 6 weeks (1.5% vs 2.9%) and 6 months (3.1% vs 1.4%), with no significant difference between groups (absolute difference at 6 weeks 1.4%, p = 0.65).

All patients should continue on low-dose aspirin therapy (3-5 mg/kg/day) for a minimum of 6 to 8 weeks after the onset of symptoms. Children should be reevaluated for the formation of coronary artery aneurysms at this point. If aneurysms are present, patients should continue on low-dose aspirin indefinitely.
For patients with coronary artery aneurysms, treatment with anticoagulant such as low-molecular-weight heparin or warfarin is needed in addition to low-dose aspirin therapy.
Approximately 10-20% of patients with KD are refractory to initial IVIG treatment, but no predictive models can accurate predict patients who will be refractory.

Current recommendations are that refractory Kawasaki Disease should be treated with a second dose of IVIG. A RCT of 48 refractory Kawasaki Disease patients found that more patients treated with IVIG + IV methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg) responded than those treated with IVIG alone (86% vs 22%; p < 0.001). For this reason the AHA in conjunction with the American Academy of Pediatrics endorsed a regime of high-dose pulse steroids (IVMP 20–30 mg/kg IV for 3 days with or without PO prednisolone taper) as an alternative to a 2nd infusion of IVIG or for retreatment of patients with recurrent fever after additional IVIG infusions. Alternatively, administration of a longer course of prednisolone (2 mg/kg/day IV divided q8h until afebrile then PO prednisolone until CRP normalized followed by 2–3-week taper) with IVIG and ASA was an acceptable regimen in their 2017 guidelines.

The role of corticosteroids in Kawasaki disease as an adjunct to IVIG for primary treatment remains controversial. Meta-analyses of studies of IVIG in combination with steroids as primary treatment for Kawasaki disease show a reduction in rates of initial treatment failure compared to those treated with IVIG alone (OR: 0.50; 95% CI: 0.32-0.79), with one meta-analysis finding a decrease in coronary abnormalities (OR: 0.30; 95% CI: 0.18-0.50), but another meta-analysis finding no change in coronary abnormalities (OR: 0.67; 95% CI: 0.35-1.28).In a randomized, open-label trial of patients with severe Kawasaki disease, patients who received IVIG + oral prednisolone (2 mg/kg) had a lower incidence of coronary abnormalities (3% vs 23%; risk difference: 0.20; 95% CI: 0.12-0.28).In the latest 2017 guidelines from the AHA and APA, has found the use of steroids is supported by evidence where the risk of refractory KD is high based on the RAISE (Kobayashi) scoring system.

Live vaccines particularly MMR should be deferred until 11 months after IVIG. If the child is high risk for measles, the immunization may be given early, but the patient will need to be reimmunized at least 11 months after IVIG was given.
There has been limited success with surgical interventions for the complications of KD.
Surgery is limited to coronary artery bypass grafts in obstructive coronary artery lesions.
Cardiac catheter intervention techniques such as balloon angioplasty, rotational ablation, and stent placement have been performed with some success.
On rare occasions, patients have undergone cardiac transplantation when severe myocardial dysfunction was present.
Approximately 10% of patients will have persistent fevers despite initial treatment with IVIG. Treatment failure is defined as fever for 36 hours or longer after completion of therapy with IVIG.

In the event of treatment failure, guidelines recommend that a second dose of IVIG be given (2 g/kg). Small studies have also shown that pulse doses of methylprednisolone are effective in the treatment of refractory KD.
Additional therapies suggested for refractory KD have included ulinastatin abciximab, infliximab plasma exchange, and cytotoxic agents.
Hospitalization is necessary for all patients requiring IVIG. Patients should remain in the hospital until afebrile or second dose of IVIG is completed.

All patients with KD should be referred to a pediatric cardiologist for initial echocardiogram and long-term followup. Length of followup will vary depending on the severity of the disease and extent of cardiac involvement.

Most coronary aneurysms (50%-67%) resolve spontaneously within 1 to 2 years. Aneurysm regression is more likely with smaller size, age <1 year at onset, fusiform morphology, and location in the distal coronary segment. B

Unresolved aneurysms can become stenotic, can occlude, or on rare occasions can rupture. The highest risk for an MI is within the first year after the onset of the disease. Patients with KD have also been shown to have altered lipid metabolism and accelerated atherosclerosis. B
Long-term management of patients with KD is based on the overall risk for MI (). C

feature.caption: Clinical Criteria for Kawasaki Disease Guideline 6180.

tr.td: Fever ≥5 days PLUS at least 4 of the following criteria:
1. Extremity changes (e.g., erythema of palms and soles, swelling of hands and feet, desquamation of fingers and toes [2-3 weeks after onset of fever])
2. Rash (may occur early in the course of disease; maculopapular, scarletiniform, erythema multiforme-like)
4. Oral cavity changes (e.g., cracked lips, erythema, or strawberry tongue)

feature.caption: Laboratory Evaluation of Suspected KD Guideline 6180.

tr.th: Principal Laboratory Tests for Systemic Inflammation

tr.td: Urinalysis with ≥10 white blood cells/high-power field

feature.caption: Risk Stratification and Long-Term Management of KD Guideline 6180.

list.listitem: No aspirin therapy or restricted physical activity following the initial 6-8 weeks of treatment
Assessment and cardiovascular risk counseling every 5 years

tr.td: II. Coronary arteries show transient changes that have resolved by 6-8 weeks

list.listitem: No aspirin therapy or restricted physical activity after the initial 6-8 weeks of treatment
Assessment and cardiovascular risk counseling every 3-5 years

tr.td: III. Small or medium-sized aneurysms in a major coronary artery

list.listitem: Long-term therapy with low-dose aspirin
Annual echocardiogram and electrocardiogram by a pediatric cardiologist
Recommendations for physical activity will be guided by stress testing with myocardial perfusion imaging every 2 years in patients older than 10 years
Patients on aspirin therapy should avoid high-impact and collision sports

tr.td: IV. One or more giant aneurysms or complex aneurysms within the same coronary artery

list.listitem: Long-term therapy with low-dose aspirin
Addition of anticoagulation therapy with warfarin or low-molecular-weight heparin
Biannual echocardiogram and electrocardiogram
Annual stress testing with myocardial perfusion imaging
Physical activity may be limited to noncontact sports if there is no evidence of stress-induced ischemia
Cardiac catheterization 6-12 months after recovery, with followup angiography if ischemia is present
Management is the same as in risk level IV
Beta blockers should be considered to reduce myocardial oxygen consumption
